content: This guide, titled Guide for Clinical Case Management and Infection Prevention and Control During a Measles Outbreak, was developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2020. It provides detailed recommendations for managing clinical cases of measles and implementing infection prevention and control (IPC) measures during outbreaks. The guide is available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-000286-9 and 978-92-4-000287-6. The guide outlines practical clinical care interventions derived from previously published WHO documents, such as the WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children and the WHO Paediatric Emergency Triage, Assessment, and Treatment guidelines. It also references international guidelines like the Surviving Sepsis Campaign. The target audience includes frontline clinicians and healthcare workers (HCWs) caring for suspected or confirmed measles cases, as well as policymakers and hospital managers responsible for ensuring safe and effective care for measles patients. Key recommendations include: 1. Reporting all suspected measles cases to public health authorities as mandated. 2. Updating IPC guidelines to include specific measures and airborne precautions for measles. 3. Ensuring all HCWs have evidence of measles immunity, with two doses of measles-containing vaccine recommended if no immunity evidence exists. 4. Prioritizing hospitalization and airborne precautions for patients with clinical warning signs, while non-severe cases should receive outpatient treatment, home isolation, and vitamin A supplementation. 5. Admitting suspected measles cases to facilities with isolation capacity, preferably single rooms, or cohorting patients in confined areas if single rooms are unavailable. 6. Administering a third dose of vitamin A 4–6 weeks later if clinical signs of vitamin A deficiency, such as xerophthalmia, are present. 7. Considering vitamin A supplementation in adults with measles, particularly in populations with suspected vitamin A deficiency, using lower but more frequent doses for women of reproductive age. 8. Providing careful care of eyes, mouth, and skin to prevent secondary infections and ensuring adequate nutrition. 9. Managing severe manifestations or complications of measles using standard care guidelines, including local or national antibiotic guidelines when available. 10. Avoiding routine prophylactic antibiotics but considering early empiric antibiotics for suspected secondary bacterial infections. 11. Recognizing insufficient evidence to recommend routine antiviral use (e.g., ribavirin) for measles. 12. Collaborating with public health authorities to evaluate exposed HCWs, patients, and visitors for measles immunity and administering post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) as necessary. The guide aims to reduce measles morbidity and mortality by ensuring early and adequate treatment and clinical case management. It also emphasizes the importance of IPC measures to prevent HCW infections, reduce transmission in healthcare settings, and protect vulnerable populations. Clinical management and IPC measures should not be delayed while awaiting laboratory confirmation of measles. Measles is one of the most contagious human diseases, caused by a paramyxovirus of the genus Morbillivirus. Transmission occurs primarily through large respiratory droplets, with airborne transmission via aerosolized droplet nuclei documented in closed areas for up to two hours after an infected person has left. The incubation period for measles is typically 10–14 days (range 7–23 days) from exposure to fever onset. Clinical presentation includes prodromal fever, rash, cough, conjunctivitis, coryza, and Koplik’s spots on the buccal mucosa. The characteristic erythematous maculopapular rash appears 2–4 days after prodrome onset, starting on the face and becoming generalized, lasting 4–7 days. Skin peeling is common after rash resolution. Complications of measles often involve the respiratory and digestive tracts, including otitis media, pneumonia, croup, diarrhea, and stomatitis. Dehydration may result from reduced oral intake or increased losses from diarrhea. Measles can also lead to febrile seizures, post-infectious encephalitis, and vitamin A deficiency-related conditions like xerophthalmia, keratitis, and keratomalacia. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a progressive degenerative brain disease, occurs in 5–10 cases per million reported measles cases, on average seven years after acute measles. Measles during pregnancy is associated with increased risks of miscarriage, preterm birth, low birth weight, and maternal death. In populations with malnutrition, overcrowding, and limited healthcare access, measles mortality can reach 2–15%. Case definitions for public health surveillance include: Suspected measles case: A patient with fever and maculopapular rash or suspected measles by a healthcare worker. Laboratory-confirmed measles: A suspected case confirmed positive by a proficient laboratory, excluding vaccine-associated illness. Epidemiologically linked measles: A suspected case not confirmed by a laboratory but geographically and temporally related to a laboratory-confirmed case. Clinically compatible measles: A suspected case with fever, maculopapular rash, and at least one of cough, coryza, or conjunctivitis, without adequate clinical specimens or epidemiological linkage to a confirmed case. A single laboratory-confirmed measles case in an elimination setting should trigger an aggressive public health investigation and response.
